access_patterns.description: Read one notification by id.
Read the search data rows of a list of posts by post_id (33 statements that differ in IN-list length), one BatchGetItem of up to 100 keys.
Delete the upload references of one target (target_type and target_id): a Query on the target_ref partition key, then BatchWriteItem deletes of the returned keys.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=target_ref (Query), then DeleteRequest on PK=target_ref AND SK=upload_id

access_patterns.description: Delete every quote row of one post: a Query on the post_id partition key, then BatchWriteItem deletes of the returned keys.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=post_id (Query), then DeleteRequest on PK=post_id AND SK=quoted_post_id

access_patterns.description: Read one group by id with the 39 columns the query selects.
Existence check for any score of one reviewable_score_type: Query with Limit 1 on the ScoresByType index.
Read one avatar row by id.
List the tags (id, name, slug) of one category from the category_tags items, which carry the tag name and slug.
List the tag group names of one category from the category_tag_groups items, which carry the tag group name.
Delete every view row of one user: a Query on the viewer_key partition key, then BatchWriteItem deletes of the returned keys.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=viewer_key (Query), then DeleteRequest on PK=viewer_key AND SK=view_key

access_patterns.description: Delete every poll vote of one user: a Query on the user_id partition key, then BatchWriteItem deletes of the returned keys.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id (Query), then DeleteRequest on PK=user_id AND SK=poll_vote_key

access_patterns.description: Existence check for any grant of one badge in a granted_at range: Query with Limit 1 on the BadgeGrants index.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=badge_id AND SK BETWEEN granted_at_start AND granted_at_end

access_patterns.description: Read the primary email row of one user: a GetItem on the user and the primary slot.
Read the primary email address of one user: a GetItem on the primary slot with a projection of the email attribute.
Check that an enabled badge exists for an id: a GetItem with a ConditionExpression-free read of the enabled flag, returning only the key.
Read one badge by id.
Find the action row for a user, action type, target post and acting user: a Query on the user with an SK prefix of the type, post and acting user, and a FilterExpression on target_topic_id.
Insert a user action. The application generates the id (the source returned it from a sequence).
Check whether the user has a primary email row with an id other than the given one: a GetItem on the primary slot that returns the id key attribute only; the application compares it.
Count actions of one type created after a timestamp: a Query on ActionsByType with Select=COUNT and a range on created_at.
Read one badge by id when it is enabled: a GetItem with the enabled flag checked by the application.
Read one badge by id with a row limit of one.
Count all actions of one type: a Query on ActionsByType with Select=COUNT.
Insert an email row into the user's primary or secondary slot. The key (user_id, primary) is the source's unique key, so the put fails when the slot is taken.
Delete an email row by its id: a Query on EmailsById finds the table key, then a DeleteItem removes the item.
access_patterns.key_condition: GSI PK=id, then PK=user_id AND SK=primary

access_patterns.description: Delete every action that refers to a user as owner, target or actor: a Query on the base table (user_id) and on ActionsByTargetUser and ActionsByActingUser, then BatchWriteItem deletes of the keys returned. It runs where the user is deleted, or from a DynamoDB Streams consumer on that delete, never as a Scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id; GSI ActionsByTargetUser PK=target_user_id; GSI ActionsByActingUser PK=acting_user_id

access_patterns.description: Read all email rows of one user: a Query on the user (at most two items).
Read the icon of every badge: a Query on BadgesAll, whose constant partition key holds all 55 badges, so no Scan is used.
Read one badge by its unique name: a Query on BadgesByName.

Re-align target_topic_id with the post's topic. The sweep becomes a write-time update: when a post changes topic, the post write path or a DynamoDB Streams consumer on the post item Queries ActionsByTargetPost for that post and runs a conditional UpdateItem per action.
access_patterns.key_condition: GSI PK=target_post_id, then PK=user_id AND SK=action_key

access_patterns.description: Remove repeated actions for a post: a Query on ActionsByTargetPost for the post, then BatchWriteItem deletes of every item beyond the first per (user_id, action_type, acting_user_id), run from the action write path or a DynamoDB Streams consumer, never as a Scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: GSI PK=target_post_id, then PK=user_id AND SK=action_key

access_patterns.description: Reads the non-deleted post with a given post_number in each of up to 5 topics: one Query per topic on the PostsByTopic index, with a filter that the post has no deleted_at.
Reads one post by post_id; topic_id, post_type (in a list of 3 values) and the absence of deleted_at are filter expressions on the item. The source ORDER BY sort_order orders at most one item.
Reads the non-deleted post with a given post_number in one topic (Limit 1) from the PostsByTopic index.
Reads one non-deleted post by post_id; the absence of deleted_at is a filter expression.
Reads the outbound_message_id of one post by post_id; the application builds the message id string around it.
Reads one non-deleted post by post_id; topic_id and the absence of deleted_at are filter expressions on the item.

Finds the posts that a given reply post answers: a Query on post_replies by reply_post_id returns the post_ids, then the application reads each post with BatchGetItem on posts (the 2 steps replace the join) and drops deleted posts with a filter; the application orders the result by post_id descending.

Reads the first post after the user's last read post in a topic (Limit 1): the application gets last_read_post_number from topic_users, then runs a Query on PostsByTopic with SK > last_read_post_number and a filter on post_type and no deleted_at; the notification conditions (reply_to_user_id, topic, category and tag notification levels) are checked by the application from topic_users, category_users, tag_users and the topic_tags items of the topic.
Finds the post_id of the non-deleted post with a given post_number and post_type in one topic (Limit 1) from the PostsByTopic index.
Finds the user id for a lowercase username through the UsersByUsernameLower index on the users placeholder table.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=username_lower (merged design: key attribute username_lower is unique_key)

access_patterns.description: Read one topic by id with all attributes.
Read one topic by id that is not soft-deleted (three statements of one pattern). GetItem returns the item and the application discards it when deleted_at is set.
Existence check of one post timing by topic, post number and user.
Read a user's live actions on one post (eight statements of one pattern). Query on the user with a post_id prefix on the sort key and a filter on deleted_at being absent.
Read id, title and slug of several non-deleted topics by an IN list of ids (34 statements of one pattern): one BatchGetItem of up to 100 keys; the application drops items with deleted_at set.
Existence check of a non-deleted topic with a given archetype (two statements of one pattern): GetItem on the id, the application compares archetype and deleted_at.
Insert a post timing, ignoring it when the topic, post number and user already have one (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING).
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id AND SK=topic_post (item written with topic_id, post_number, user_id, msecs)

access_patterns.description: Add elapsed milliseconds to an existing post timing with an atomic ADD; the condition keeps the update from creating a missing item, as the source UPDATE does.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id AND SK=topic_post; SET msecs = msecs + :n

access_patterns.description: Read a topic's highest post number, a strongly consistent GetItem because callers use it to number the next post.
Check whether any live action of a type exists: Query with Limit on the type GSI, filtered on deleted_at being absent, paged until one item passes or the partition ends.
Read one upload by id.

Find an upload by url with id above a bound, old enough and past its retain_hours, in id order with a limit: Query on the url GSI with a sort-key range on upload_id; retain_hours and created_at conditions are filter expressions.
Read the post number of one timing by topic, user and post number.
Delete every post timing of a user: Query on the partition key user_id, then BatchWriteItem deletes of up to 25 keys per call (no Scan).
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id (Query for the keys, then DeleteRequest per SK)

access_patterns.description: Read a user's live actions in id order with a limit: Query on the partition key user_id with a deleted_at filter; the application orders the user's items by id.
Delete every action of a user: Query on the base partition key user_id (the key-scoped write's key), then BatchWriteItem deletes of up to 25 keys per call (no Scan).
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id (Query for the keys, then DeleteRequest per SK)

access_patterns.description: Read an upload by sha1: GetItem on the sha1 sentinel item, which carries the upload id, then GetItem on the upload item.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=upload_key ('SHA1#{sha1}') AND SK=record_type ('SHA1'), then PK=upload_key ('UPLOAD#{upload_id}') AND SK=record_type ('UPLOAD')

access_patterns.description: Insert an upload and its sha1 sentinel in one TransactWriteItems; each Put carries attribute_not_exists so a taken sha1 cancels the insert. The application generates the id.
access_patterns.key_condition: Put PK=upload_key ('UPLOAD#{id}') SK=record_type ('UPLOAD'); Put PK=upload_key ('SHA1#{sha1}') SK=record_type ('SHA1')

access_patterns.description: Set dominant_color on an existing upload by id.
Look up one user by lowercase username (login, mention and profile routes). Query on the UsersByUsernameLower GSI, which projects the whole item.
Load users by id (post authors, mentions, serializers). The source returns 5.3 rows per call on average, so the application sends the ids as one BatchGetItem on the USER items.
Load one user by id (LIMIT 1).

List the ids of the users a user has muted. The source joins muted_users to users only to return users.id, which equals muted_users.muted_user_id, so one Query on the user's item collection replaces the join.
Update user activity timestamps (updated_at, last_posted_at) by id. None of these attributes is a key or a unique value, so no sentinel changes.

Create a user. One TransactWriteItems puts the USER item and the sentinel items for username, username_lower and, when present, secure_identifier (4 items at most). A taken value cancels the whole insert. The application generates the id.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id AND SK='PROFILE'; sentinels PK=unique_key in user_unique_values

access_patterns.description: Look up one user by exact-case username on the UsersByUsername GSI.
Delete a user by id. The application first reads the USER item, then one TransactWriteItems deletes it and its sentinel items so the username values are free again.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id AND SK='PROFILE'; sentinels PK=unique_key in user_unique_values

access_patterns.description: Consistency repair of users.title, carried write. Modeled as write-time enforcement: the consumer of the stream on the badge-grant and profile items (owned by other groups) runs a conditional UpdateItem on the USER item by user_id when a granted title badge is revoked or disabled. No Scan and no batch sweep.

Orphan clean-up of users.uploaded_avatar_id, carried write. When an upload is removed, a consumer of the uploads stream (owned by another group) queries the sparse UsersByUploadedAvatar GSI with that upload id and runs a conditional UpdateItem on each USER item to reset uploaded_avatar_id. No Scan.
Delete every group request of one user: Query the RequestsByUser index on user_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by id.
Delete every review claim of one user: Query the ClaimsByUser index on user_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by id.
Retention delete of upload stubs in one status older than a cutoff: Query the StubsByStatus index on status with created_at <= cutoff, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by id.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=status AND SK<=created_at cutoff (StubsByStatus), then delete PK=id

access_patterns.description: Read the review groups of a post type for up to 8 categories: one Query per category id with the post type as the sort key prefix.
List the name and id of every LLM model: Query the AllModels index on its constant partition value, which holds all 10 items, instead of a Scan.
Read the SVG sprite of one theme by theme_id.
Read one user upload link by user_id and upload_id.
Delete all fragment embeddings of one model: Query PK=model_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by key.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=model_id, then delete PK=model_id AND SK=strategy_fragment

access_patterns.description: Delete all topic embeddings of one model: Query PK=model_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by key.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=model_id, then delete PK=model_id AND SK=strategy_topic

access_patterns.description: Delete all post embeddings of one model: Query PK=model_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by key.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=model_id, then delete PK=model_id AND SK=strategy_post

access_patterns.description: Read the shared draft of one topic by topic_id (GetItem on the natural key).
Read the full stats item of one user by user_id.
Read first_unread_at of one user by user_id (GetItem with a projection expression).
List the ids of all user fields. The 14 definitions share one partition key value, so the read is a Query on that value, not a Scan.

List the users one user allows to send private messages. A Query on allowed_pm_users returns the allowed user ids; the application resolves the usernames with a BatchGetItem on the users table that group 1 owns.
List the tag ids a user follows at one notification level: Query on user_id with a FilterExpression on notification_level.
Upsert the search text of one user (PutItem replaces the item for the user_id key, as the source ON CONFLICT does).
Read the settings of one category by category_id.
Existence check: does the user have a timing with starts_at <= now and ends_at > now. Query on user_id with a FilterExpression on both timestamps.
Read the bookmark of one user for one bookmarkable (type and id) with GetItem on user_id and bookmarkable_key.
Read the shared drafts of a list of topics (IN list of up to 36 ids in the sampled statements) with BatchGetItem on topic_id; one call holds up to 100 keys.
Set last_used_at on one API key by id. The condition keeps the update from creating an item for an unknown id.
Upsert the search text of one topic (PutItem replaces the item for the topic_id key, as the source ON CONFLICT does).
Existence check: is the user a member of the group. GetItem on group_id and user_id.

Highest notification level (levels in a given pair) a user has on the tags of one topic. The application reads the topic's tag ids from topic_tags (group 2 owns it), then BatchGetItem on tag_users with user_id and each tag_id, and keeps the highest matching notification_level.

Orphan clean-up modeled by intent: a DynamoDB Streams consumer on the topics table deletes the topic_search_data item (DeleteItem on topic_id) when a topic is removed or its deleted_at is set past the retention date. The anti-join sweep is not a Scan.
Read the anonymous account of a master user by master_user_id; the application checks the active attribute on the returned item.
Delete all daily like rows of one user: Query on user_id (key-scoped write served by the base table key), then BatchWriteItem deletes of the returned keys.
Delete the search item of one user by user_id.
List all user field definitions in position order. Query on the shared partition key value; the application sorts the 14 returned items by position.
Insert one scheduler run record with an application-generated id and a TTL attribute.
Update duration, live slots at finish and success of the run record by id.
Read all custom fields of one category in id order.
Read the trackers of one identifier whose target differs from a given value.
Read the active timer of one timerable by type and public_type.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=timerable_id AND FilterExpression type = :type AND public_type = :public_type AND attribute_not_exists(deleted_at)

access_patterns.description: Read the custom fields of one post whose name is in a list of up to 7 names, in id order.
Read the active timer of one timerable by type and status_type.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=timerable_id AND FilterExpression type = :type AND status_type = :status_type AND attribute_not_exists(deleted_at)

access_patterns.description: Read one tracker by identifier and target.
Read active timers of a type whose execute_at is due, from the sparse DueTimersByType index.
Read all custom fields of one post in id order.
Update last_run_at, next_run_at and last_success_at of the tracker. The caller holds the loaded item, so it addresses the update by identifier and target.
Read custom fields for up to 7 categories filtered by up to 10 names: one Query per category with a name filter.
Read every attribute of all custom fields of one post.
Insert a custom field and skip it when the item already exists (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING).
Find the category ids that carry a custom field with a given name and value, through the CategoriesByNameValue index.
Read the first active timers of a type; the index returns them in execute_at order and the application orders the few results by id.
Insert a tracker; the identifier and target pair must be new.
Retention delete of runs older than the cut-off: served by DynamoDB Time to Live on expires_at, with no Scan and no write cost.
access_patterns.key_condition: TTL on expires_at (items deleted by DynamoDB in the background)

access_patterns.description: Read the custom fields named in a short list for up to five topics: one Query per topic_id, with a FilterExpression on name; the application merges the results and orders them by id (the sort key).
Existence check: does any watched word have this action. Query with Limit 1 and a key-only projection.
Read every custom field of one topic, ordered by id: Query on the topic_id partition, whose sort key is id.
Read the vote count row of one topic with Limit 1 through the VotesByTopic index.
Read the vote count rows of up to five topics: one Query per topic_id on the VotesByTopic index.
Existence check for one locale and translation key: GetItem on the full key with a key-only projection.
Read the notification schedule of one user: Query on the user_id partition with Limit 1.
Read one badge type by id: GetItem.
Read one plugin store row by plugin name and key: GetItem.
Record an applied migration version. The source primary key rejects a duplicate version, so the put carries the same guard.
Read one color scheme by id; the application discards the item unless remote_copy equals the requested value (GetItem accepts no filter).
Read the words of one action in id order: Query on the action partition, whose sort key is id.
Read one badge type by id with a row limit: GetItem.
Read all overrides of one locale: Query on the locale partition.
Read every applied version in order: Query on the single migration_set partition, whose sort key is version; paginated at 1 MB per page.
Read one plugin store row by plugin name and key: GetItem.
Insert a skipped email log item with an application-generated id and the expires_at epoch attribute that the retention TTL reads.
Read one color scheme by id: GetItem.
Retention delete served by Time to Live on the expires_at attribute: DynamoDB removes expired items in the background at no write cost, and no Scan or batch delete runs.
access_patterns.key_condition: TTL on expires_at (items removed by DynamoDB)

access_patterns.description: Read all schedules by enabled value through the EnabledSchedules index (enabled_flag 1 or 0).
Insert one search log row; the application generates the id because DynamoDB has no sequence.
Read the password record of one user by user_id (unique in the source).
Insert one unsubscribe key, keyed by the key value itself, with an expires_at attribute for TTL.
List the upcoming change names of one event type in created_at order, served by the EventsByType index.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=event_type AND SK ascending by created_at

access_patterns.description: List every job name. A Query on the OnceoffByScope index with the constant partition value ONCEOFF replaces the full-table read.
Read the events of one type for up to 12 named upcoming changes: a BatchGetItem on the (name, event_type) key; the application sorts the few results by created_at.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=upcoming_change_name AND SK=event_type (one key per name)

access_patterns.description: Read one webhook event type by id.
Update created_at and term of one search log by id; expires_at is recomputed from the new created_at in the same UpdateItem.
Read the modifier set of one theme by theme_id; the IS NOT NULL test on a modifier column is applied by the application to the returned item.
Insert the password record of a user; user_id is the table key, so its unique constraint is enforced by the condition.
Delete a password record. The caller holds the loaded record and deletes by user_id; a caller that has only the id first reads the user_id from the PasswordsById index.
Insert one webhook event type with its explicit id.
Copy the hook links of one event type to another: a Query on the source event type's partition, then a BatchWriteItem of the copied items under the new event type.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=web_hook_event_type_id (read source partition, write target partition)

access_patterns.description: Check whether one theme has only_theme_color_schemes set: GetItem by theme_id, the flag compared by the application.
Retention delete of old unsubscribe keys, served by Time to Live on expires_at; no application call runs.
Read the modifier set of one theme by theme_id.
Retention delete of old search logs, served by Time to Live on expires_at; no application call runs.
Insert one event; the (upcoming_change_name, event_type) key carries the source's unique index, so the condition enforces it.
Insert one once-off job record with an application-generated id.
Existence check for one job name: Query on OnceoffByScope with PK=ONCEOFF and SK=job_name.
Read one site setting by name (all attributes).
Load every setting (name, data_type, value) with a Query on the constant-partition index AllSettings instead of a Scan.
Read the value of one setting by name.
Delete a setting by name.
Rename a setting. The name is the table key, so the rename deletes the old item and puts the new one in one TransactWriteItems.
access_patterns.condition_expression: attribute_exists(name) on the delete of the old name; attribute_not_exists(name) on the put of the new name

access_patterns.description: Copy a setting under a new name: GetItem on the source name, then PutItem of the copy.
Update a setting's value and updated_at by id. A Query on the SettingsById index finds the name, then UpdateItem on the base table writes the item.
Insert a new setting; the application generates the id.
Rename a setting only when the new name is free: delete the old item and put the new one in one TransactWriteItems.
access_patterns.condition_expression: attribute_exists(name) on the delete of the old name; attribute_not_exists(name) on the put of the new name

access_patterns.description: Read one user's state for one topic by the full table key.
Update last_emailed_post_number on one existing topic_users row addressed by topic_id and user_id. The condition keeps the source UPDATE semantics: a missing row is not created.
Read one user's state for a list of topics (IN lists of varying length): one BatchGetItem of (topic_id, user_id) keys, split into calls of at most 100 keys.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=topic_id AND SK=user_id for each requested topic_id

access_patterns.description: Reviewables of one topic with a given status and type, oldest first. target_created_by_id is a filter on the Query.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=topic_id AND SK status=:s AND type=:t, ordered by created_at ascending; FilterExpression target_created_by_id=:u

access_patterns.description: User ids of one topic whose last_read_post_number is at least a given post number: a Query on the topic partition with a FilterExpression.

Existence check for one user and topic: the key condition names the row and a FilterExpression holds notifications_reason_id absent, or notification_level between the two bounds. An empty result means false.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=topic_id AND SK=user_id; FilterExpression attribute_not_exists(notifications_reason_id) OR (notification_level < :hi AND notification_level > :lo)

access_patterns.description: Create the topic_users row for a user and topic. The (topic_id, user_id) table key carries the source's unique constraint, so the conditional Put rejects a duplicate.
Existence check for one user and topic at a given notification_level: the key condition names the row and a FilterExpression holds the level.

Ids of reviewables with a given status, score at or above a bound and latest_score below a bound. The index orders by score; latest_score is a FilterExpression; the application sorts the ids descending.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=status AND SK score >= :s; FilterExpression latest_score < :t

access_patterns.description: Ids of reviewables with a given type and status created before a bound: a Query on the status partition with created_at as range and type as a FilterExpression.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=status AND SK created_at < :t; FilterExpression type = :type

access_patterns.description: Key-scoped bulk update for one user: Query TopicUsersByUser for the user's rows, filter attribute_not_exists(notifications_reason_id), then UpdateItem notification_level on each row from the projected total_msecs_viewed, in batches of parallel UpdateItem calls. Never a Scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id; FilterExpression attribute_not_exists(notifications_reason_id); then UpdateItem on PK=topic_id AND SK=user_id for each row

access_patterns.description: Key-scoped delete of every topic_users row of one user: Query TopicUsersByUser for the keys, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest of (topic_id, user_id) in batches of 25. Never a Scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id; then BatchWriteItem delete on PK=topic_id AND SK=user_id

access_patterns.description: Key-scoped delete of every reviewable created by one user: Query ReviewablesByCreator for the ids, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by id in batches of 25. Never a Scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=created_by_id; then BatchWriteItem delete on PK=id

access_patterns.description: Reviewable of a given type and status for one target (target_type and target_id), first match.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=target_type AND target_id AND SK type=:type AND status=:s; Limit 1

access_patterns.description: Oldest reviewables with a given status created before a bound, limited to a page: a Query on the status partition ordered by created_at.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=status AND SK created_at < :t, ascending, Limit :n

access_patterns.description: Count of reviewables with a given status and score above a bound: a Query on the status partition with Select=COUNT.
List the scopes of one API key.
Find a user's associated account for one provider.

Existence check for a live (not deleted) embed of a topic. The Query takes the topic_id partition key and a filter attribute_not_exists(deleted_at); a NULL deleted_at is stored as an absent attribute.
Upsert of the daily request counter: UpdateItem with ADD count :n on the item keyed by date and req_type creates the item when absent, so the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE needs no condition.
Existence check for an enabled second factor of one method for a user, as a Query on user_id with a filter on method and enabled.
List the auth tokens of one user.
List the active (not revoked) API keys of a user: Query on user_id with filter attribute_not_exists(revoked_at).
New email addresses of a user's change requests whose change_state differs from a given state: Query on user_id with a filter on change_state.
Record one migration run.
Read every embeddable host. The 22 rows share the constant partition key value scope=embeddable_hosts, so the read is one Query on a single item collection and never a Scan.
Record composer statistics for a post.
Look up the counter row of one date and user agent.
Find the directory column by name and type that has no icon: Query on the name and type GSI with filter attribute_not_exists(icon), limit 1.
Read a sitemap by name.
Add a color to a color scheme.
List the colors of one color scheme in id order (the sort key).
Read one AI agent by id.
Read one screened IP address by id.

Create an AI agent. One TransactWriteItems puts the agent item (attribute_not_exists(id)) and the name sentinel item in ai_agent_names (attribute_not_exists(name)); a taken name cancels the whole insert.
access_patterns.condition_expression: attribute_not_exists(id) on the agent Put AND attribute_not_exists(name) on the sentinel Put

access_patterns.description: List screened IP addresses of one action type last matched (or, never matched, created) before a cutoff. match_sort_at holds last_match_at, or created_at when last_match_at is NULL, which is the source's OR condition exactly.
Fetch the solved-topic rows for an IN list of up to 5 topic ids with one BatchGetItem on the topic_id key.
Fetch the solved-topic row of one topic with GetItem on topic_id.
Read the draft sequence number of one user and draft key with GetItem.
Fetch the category notification row of one user and category with GetItem.
Find which of up to 5 topics a user dismissed with one BatchGetItem on (user_id, topic_id) keys.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id AND SK=topic_id (one key per IN-list value)

migration_notes.application_logic_required: The source trigger raises an error on INSERT or UPDATE of require_reply_approval. The application layer rejects writes to require_reply_approval and require_topic_approval, because DynamoDB has no triggers.
The source trigger raises an error on INSERT or UPDATE of require_topic_approval. The application layer rejects the write, or an IAM condition on dynamodb:Attributes denies it.

The trigger rejects changes to topic_id. The application stops writing topic_id on UpdateItem and adds the condition expression `attribute_not_exists(topic_id) OR topic_id = :topic_id` to any write that carries it.

trade_offs.description: Each source table in this group becomes its own DynamoDB table, and the surrogate id stays the key of groups, notifications, user_avatars, user_badges, tags, tag_groups and reviewable_scores.
trade_offs.impact: Queries `-3861694`, `-7052261` and `-1805966` look rows up by id, and the other candidates (groups.name, groups.incoming_email) are never looked up in this group, so a natural key adds no read path. Other groups that read these rows by id reach them through the same key.

trade_offs.description: The link tables category_tags, category_tag_groups, quoted_posts and poll_votes are keyed by the parent column their queries use (category_id, post_id, user_id) with the other id as sort key, so the source's unique indexes become the primary key. upload_references is keyed by target_ref (target_type#target_id) with upload_id as sort key, and topic_views by viewer_key (the user id, or ip# plus the address for anonymous views) with topic_id#viewed_at#ip_address as sort key.
trade_offs.impact: The surrogate id of these tables is kept as an attribute and is not a key, so a lookup by that id needs a new index. Anonymous topic views share no partition with signed-in users, and no key in this group has fewer than the source's distinct values.

trade_offs.description: The four deletes by a non-unique key column (queries `-5182200`, `-4538458`, `-4017385`, `-7736444`) run as a Query on the table's partition key followed by BatchWriteItem DeleteRequests of up to 25 items per call; upload_references puts target_type inside its target_ref partition key.
trade_offs.impact: The source runs each as one statement; DynamoDB runs a Query and one write per 25 items, with no atomicity across calls. A failed batch is retried from the unprocessed keys; no Scan is used.

trade_offs.description: The tag name, tag slug and tag group name are copied into category_tags and category_tag_groups, replacing the two joins of queries `-3427295` and `5631712`.
trade_offs.impact: Each read is one Query on category_id. A renamed tag or tag group changes the copies only when a DynamoDB Streams consumer rewrites them, so the old name is returned until that consumer applies the change.

trade_offs.description: ScoresByType (reviewable_score_type) and BadgeGrants (badge_id, granted_at) are KEYS_ONLY indexes that serve the Limit 1 existence checks of queries `-4711011` and `-2374558`, which return no attributes.
trade_offs.impact: Both keys have few distinct values, but the checks run at 0.0021 and 0.0002 requests per second, so no partition nears its limit. The indexes are eventually consistent: a score or grant is visible to the check once DynamoDB applies the base write to the index, and a caller that needs the latest write reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem.

trade_offs.description: No in-scope write inserts or changes a unique attribute (groups.name, groups.incoming_email, tags.name, the unique user_badges indexes), so no sentinel items are written; poll_votes, quoted_posts, upload_references and the category link tables enforce their unique indexes through the primary key.
trade_offs.impact: A PutItem on those link tables overwrites an existing row with the same key instead of failing; a writer that must reject duplicates adds attribute_not_exists on the key. A later write path for groups, tags or user_badges adds sentinel items in a TransactWriteItems.

trade_offs.description: Query pattern PAT-4 (33 statements with IN lists of different lengths on post_search_data.post_id) is one BatchGetItem of up to 100 keys; the tsvector column is stored as its text form and the GIN index on it is not recreated.
trade_offs.impact: A list longer than 100 post ids splits into several calls. Full text matching on search_data is not served by DynamoDB, and no query in this group uses it. The table's avg_row_size_bytes is 1960 against the 400 KB item limit, so raw_data stays inline.

trade_offs.description: The source has no row count for category_tag_groups, category_tags, poll_votes, quoted_posts, reviewable_scores, tag_groups, tags, topic_views and upload_references, so their item counts are derived from each table's size.
trade_offs.impact: Capacity and cost figures for those tables rest on that estimate; at the measured rates (at most 0.0478 requests per second for any pattern) no table or index reaches 1% of a partition limit.

trade_offs.description: user_actions is keyed by user_id with the sort key action_key (action_type, target_post_id, acting_user_id, id) instead of the source's unique index on five columns.
trade_offs.impact: That index covers target_topic_id, target_post_id and acting_user_id, which are nullable, so the source does not guarantee uniqueness and a key built from them could overwrite a legitimate row. target_topic_id is also rewritten by the consistency repair, and a key attribute cannot be updated in place. The id stays in the key, the lookup in query `26476120` is a Query on a sort-key prefix with a filter on target_topic_id, and the user delete in query `30151265` reads the base table by user_id.

trade_offs.description: user_emails is keyed by user_id and primary ('P' or 'S'), which is the source's unique index on (user_id, primary), whose columns are NOT NULL and have no predicate.
trade_offs.impact: The table key enforces the constraint, so a conditional PutItem with attribute_not_exists(user_id) replaces the source's duplicate check and no sentinel item is needed. The lookups in queries `-1544240` and `-3633820` are GetItem calls. Changing which email is primary is a delete and a put of both slots in one TransactWriteItems (2 items, within the 100-item limit), which no in-scope query performs. The table holds 48 rows, so a user has at most two items.

trade_offs.description: Deleting an email by its id alone (query `-7887291`) uses the EmailsById index to find the table key.
trade_offs.impact: The identifying key serves the user_id lookups, which run at 0.3154 requests per second for the primary read alone, against 0.0011 for the delete by id, so the id lookup is the minority and takes a KEYS_ONLY index. The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a delete of an email inserted a moment earlier within the same request reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem.

trade_offs.description: The two COUNT queries on user_actions (queries `-8883206` and `-2719095`) run as Query calls with Select=COUNT on ActionsByType (action_type, created_at).
trade_offs.impact: A count reads and bills every matching index entry (60 bytes each, 1 MB per page); the table holds 1025 rows and the counts run at 0.0127 requests per second, so a counter item is not added. The cardinality of action_type is not collected; at this rate no partition value nears a limit. A count over a much larger table moves to a counter item maintained with an atomic ADD in the write's transaction.

trade_offs.description: The delete by user_id, target_user_id or acting_user_id (query `30151265`) becomes Query calls on the base table and on ActionsByTargetUser and ActionsByActingUser followed by BatchWriteItem deletes.
trade_offs.impact: Both indexes are sparse on a nullable attribute; the share of rows without the attribute is not collected. Each action is deleted once per key found, so a row matching several references is deleted by the first Query and the later deletes of it are no-ops. The delete runs where the user is deleted or from a DynamoDB Streams consumer on that delete, and no Scan is used.

trade_offs.description: The topic repair (query `-8208700`) and the duplicate clean-up (query `-2784383`) become write-time operations on ActionsByTargetPost instead of set-based sweeps.
trade_offs.impact: The repair reads the posts table, which another design group owns, so this design defines no posts table and writes none of its rows. The post write path or a DynamoDB Streams consumer on the post item, which the posts owner serves, Queries ActionsByTargetPost and runs a conditional UpdateItem with target_topic_id <> :topic_id per action. The duplicate clean-up Queries the same index and deletes the extra items per (user_id, action_type, acting_user_id); the action write path runs it after an insert. Neither is a Scan.

trade_offs.description: badges is keyed by id, with BadgesByName (unique name) and BadgesAll (a constant entity_name partition key) as indexes.
trade_offs.impact: Five of the six badge reads look up by id, so id is the key. The read of every icon (query `-5609072`) has no key value, so BadgesAll holds all 55 badges under one partition key value and returns the icon attribute with INCLUDE projection; at 0.0004 requests per second the value is far below the 3000 RCU limit. Name is unique and NOT NULL, but it is a rename-able display value, so it is an index and not the key. Badges are not written by any in-scope query, so no sentinel item is needed.

trade_offs.description: badges keeps the description, query and long_description text columns inline, with the other columns, in one item.
trade_offs.impact: The measured average row is 1907 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, so no column moves to S3.

trade_offs.description: Ids that the source generated from sequences (user_actions.id, user_emails.id) are generated by the application and carried by the items.
trade_offs.impact: The inserts in queries `-7300874` and `86863492` return the id in the source; the application now creates it before the PutItem, and an id collision on user_actions fails on attribute_not_exists(action_key).

trade_offs.description: posts is keyed by post_id (the source primary key) and reached by topic_id and post_number through the PostsByTopic index, which projects all attributes.
trade_offs.impact: Reads by post id (queries `5294935a`, `-9104347`, `-4931816` and the 10-statement pattern `-4105318`) total 0.49 requests per second against 0.42 for topic and post number reads, and other groups read posts by the source id, so the id stays the table key. The topic and post_number lookups read the index, which lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a read that must see a just-written post reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem. The surrogate id is kept rather than the natural pair (topic_id, post_number) because that pair is unique but the id-only lookups would then need an index on every read.

trade_offs.description: The join of posts and post_replies in query `5884248130138369695` becomes a Query on post_replies by reply_post_id followed by a BatchGetItem on posts.
trade_offs.impact: The read costs 2 requests instead of 1 join; the BatchGetItem on posts adds about 0.5 read units per returned post at 0.0478 requests per second, which is under 0.03 read units per second and is not listed separately in the capacity entries. post_replies is keyed by (reply_post_id, post_id), the unique pair of the source; its source columns are nullable and a row with a null in either column is not migrated because it cannot be keyed.

trade_offs.description: Query `-5272548625492493566` is served as a Query on PostsByTopic (SK greater than the last read post number, Limit 1) plus application checks against topic_users, category_users, tag_users and topic_tags.
trade_offs.impact: The application reads the user's topic_users, category_users and tag_users items by key and the topic's topic_tags items (Query on topic_id), then evaluates the OR of the notification conditions itself; at 0.0041 requests per second the extra reads are negligible. The three user tables belong to other design groups and are read, never written, by this group; topic_tags items are read by this group and are keyed by (topic_id, tag_id).

trade_offs.description: The users table is a placeholder owned by another design group, keyed by user_id, with the UsersByUsernameLower index on username_lower for query `8270933069653201035`.
trade_offs.impact: username_lower is unique in the source (index_users_on_username_lower) but no in-scope write of this group sets it, so no sentinel item is written here; the owning group designs the user writes and any uniqueness guard. The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it.

trade_offs.description: The raw and cooked text columns stay inline in the posts item; the posts avg_row_size_bytes is 2809 against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: At 2809 bytes an average post is far under the limit, so no S3 offload is needed; a single post with a very large body would need the pointer approach if one approaches 400 KB. Each post read costs 0.5 read units (one 4 KB step, eventually consistent).

trade_offs.description: The row counts of post_replies and topic_tags are not collected; the item counts of 0 for these tables are the assumed figures from design_metrics, derived from table size over the item size.
trade_offs.impact: The capacity figures for these 2 tables rest on that derived count and are re-checked once the migration reports the loaded item counts.

trade_offs.description: post_actions is keyed by user_id with a sort key of post_id, post_action_type_id and targets_topic, not by the generated id.
trade_offs.impact: The user-scoped delete (query `-1932152331896383119`) and the per-user reads (queries `7574554412558242017` and `6946259433174667106`) are Queries on the base partition key. The sort key repeats the source unique index on user_id, post_action_type_id, post_id and targets_topic, so a PutItem cannot overwrite a different action. The id stays an attribute. A read by post_id alone has no key and needs a GSI from the group that issues it. Read order by id for the user-ordered read is applied by the application over one user's items.

trade_offs.description: Deleting all actions or all timings of a user is a Query on the partition key followed by BatchWriteItem calls of up to 25 deletes, not one SQL DELETE.
trade_offs.impact: The delete is not atomic across batches; a failed batch is retried from the Query result, and deleting an already-deleted key succeeds. Rates are 0.0006 requests per second each.

trade_offs.description: PostActionsByType serves the existence check by post_action_type_id (query `-4753344182186834428`), projects deleted_at and is filtered on it.
trade_offs.impact: A FilterExpression is applied after the read, so the check pages until an item with no deleted_at passes. post_action_type_id has few distinct values, but the check runs 0.0021 times per second and the table holds 11 rows (derived from the table size), so no partition value nears a limit. The GSI lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it.

trade_offs.description: post_timings is keyed by user_id with a sort key topic_id#post_number, which covers the source unique key on topic_id, post_number and user_id.
trade_offs.impact: Every pattern in this group supplies the full key or only the user, so all are GetItem, PutItem, UpdateItem or a base-table Query. The insert uses attribute_not_exists to keep ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; the msecs update is an atomic ADD guarded by attribute_exists so it never creates an item. A user with many timings holds them in one partition; 685 rows in total at 231 bytes each stay far below the partition limits.

trade_offs.description: topics keeps the generated id as the partition key; external_id (unique, nullable) is not used as the key.
trade_offs.impact: All topic reads in this group (queries `6746886374591153495`, `6004114026531250967`, `6521797610071425627`, `-6743783899260303753`, `5265701797568864180`) look up by id, and other groups read topics by the source id. No in-scope write sets external_id, so no sentinel item is written for it. The deleted_at conditions are applied by the application on the item GetItem and BatchGetItem return (the item averages 2374 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, so every column stays inline). The 34-statement IN-list pattern becomes one BatchGetItem of up to 100 keys.

trade_offs.description: The highest_post_number read (query `5265701797568864180`) is a strongly consistent GetItem; all other topic reads are eventually consistent.
trade_offs.impact: A strongly consistent read costs 1 read unit per 4 KB instead of 0.5, 0.007 units per second at this rate. The other reads can return a topic up to about one second behind a write to its replicas.

trade_offs.description: The sha1 unique index on uploads is enforced with a sentinel item (partition key SHA1#<sha1>) written with the upload in one TransactWriteItems with attribute_not_exists on both Puts.
trade_offs.impact: An insert is 2 items, well below the 100-item transaction limit, and costs two write units per 1 KB per item (prepare and commit), 0.0001 inserts per second. A canceled transaction still consumes them. Uploads with a null sha1 write no sentinel. The sha1 lookup (query `4098849079692402`) is a GetItem on the sentinel then a GetItem on the upload. The uploads item_count counts the 9 upload rows; up to 9 sentinel items are added.

trade_offs.description: UploadsByUrl indexes url with upload_id as sort key and projects all attributes, serving query `-8400597078852665671`.
trade_offs.impact: The retain_hours and created_at conditions run as filter expressions on the items read for one url. Every update of an upload (such as dominant_color, query `7236001677532908817`) is also written to the index, 3 write units per item at 0.0001 requests per second. Sentinel items have no url and stay out of the index.

trade_offs.description: The source generates uploads.id with a sequence; the application generates it on insert, and the uploads item keeps the origin column inline.
trade_offs.impact: Query `-1915920121626532152` returned the id from the database; the application now supplies it before the transaction. The origin column is TEXT capped at 2000 characters in the size estimate; the average uploads item is 2294 bytes against the 400 KB limit, so it stays inline. The uploads, post_actions and reviewable_scores row counts are derived from table sizes.

trade_offs.description: The UNION probe over post_actions and reviewable_scores (query `4582415969089977699`) is of type OTHER and no access pattern is designed for it; reviewable_scores, owned by another group, needs no placeholder here.
trade_offs.impact: No table in this group depends on writes to reviewable_scores.

trade_offs.description: The users table keeps the source id as its partition key (user_id) and serves username lookups through the UsersByUsernameLower and UsersByUsername GSIs.
trade_offs.impact: Username_lower is unique and not null, and its lookup (query `-7551067248247426933`, 3.27 requests per second) runs more often than the id lookups (1.23 per second together), but a username can be renamed and a key cannot be updated in place: a rename would be a delete and a put of the whole item collection. Other groups read users by id, so the id stays in the key. Username lookups are eventually consistent GSI reads.

trade_offs.description: Users and muted_users share one item collection keyed by user_id: USER items use SK `PROFILE`, MUTED_USER items use SK `MUTED#{muted_user_id}`. The source join in query `-4209837464724120931` returns only users.id, which equals muted_users.muted_user_id, so one Query on the collection serves it.
trade_offs.impact: The mute list is read with one Query and no join. The muted_users row_count is derived from the table's size (0.02 MB), not collected. The surrogate muted_users.id is not stored, because the (user_id, muted_user_id) pair identifies a mute and both unique indexes of the source cover that pair. The reverse lookup by muted_user_id has no query in scope and no GSI.

trade_offs.description: Three GSIs on users: UsersByUsernameLower and UsersByUsername project ALL; UsersByUploadedAvatar is sparse and projects keys only.
trade_offs.impact: The two username indexes serve reads that return the whole item (query `-7551067248247426933` and query `8063656422256296209`), so no base-table fetch is needed. Every write to a USER item is also written to both ALL indexes (3 write units per index for the 2,125-byte item), about 0.05 write units per second each at the design rate, far under 1,000. UsersByUploadedAvatar holds only items with an avatar, finds the users to repair for query `8321624443266976557`, and is written only when that attribute changes. The share of users without an avatar is not collected.

trade_offs.description: Carried writes query `2150880814507944816` (title repair) and query `8321624443266976557` (orphan avatar reference) are modeled as write-time enforcement through stream consumers with conditional UpdateItem on the USER item, not as set-based sweeps.
trade_offs.impact: The consumers react to badge-grant and profile changes and to upload removals, which other groups own (public.badges, public.user_badges, public.user_profiles, public.uploads). This group defines no placeholder for them and writes none of their rows; their owners' tables must emit the stream events. Until a consumer processes an event the title or avatar reference stays stale, bounded by the stream's 24-hour retention. The source's all-rows sweep has no DynamoDB equivalent without a Scan, and none is designed.

trade_offs.description: Query `2274020325713084590` and its pattern members return 5.3 rows per call on average for a filter on one id, so the pattern is a BatchGetItem over the ids the caller holds.
trade_offs.impact: Each call reads about 5.3 USER items at 0.5 read unit each (2,125 bytes rounds to 4 KB), 1.76 read units per second in total. A batch holds up to 100 keys and 16 MB.

trade_offs.description: The source id columns (users.id, muted_users.id) come from sequences; the application generates user ids for new USER items.
trade_offs.impact: The id must be unique across concurrent sign-ups: the conditional put on user_id rejects a duplicate. Existing ids are copied unchanged.

trade_offs.description: A users row averages 4,155 bytes in the source (2,115 bytes by the schema rule) and stays inline with no S3 offload.
trade_offs.impact: The item is far under the 400 KB limit and costs 3 write units per write and 0.5 read unit per read. The ip_address and registration_ip_address inet columns are stored as strings.

trade_offs.description: Deletes by a non-key column (queries `45187686` on group_requests.user_id and `60515295` on reviewable_claimed_topics.user_id) are served by a Query on a GSI keyed on user_id followed by BatchWriteItem deletes.
trade_offs.impact: The single DELETE statement becomes a read of the user's keys and a batch of deletes in 25-item calls; the two steps are not atomic, and a retry deletes whatever remains. Both tables hold 31 and 0 assumed rows, so one user's batch is a single call.

trade_offs.description: Both tables stay keyed on the surrogate id because no in-scope query reads them by a natural key; user_id is a GSI partition key (a user has few rows, so the value is not hot). The group_requests user_id column is nullable, so rows without it are absent from RequestsByUser.
trade_offs.impact: Other groups that read these rows by the source id keep a direct GetItem. The unique (group_id, user_id) pair of group_requests is not enforced by DynamoDB because no in-scope write inserts or changes it.

trade_offs.description: The retention delete of query `11537686` (status = x AND created_at <= cutoff) uses the StubsByStatus GSI with status as partition key and created_at as sort key, then a batch delete by id.
trade_offs.impact: Status has few distinct values, so one status value holds all matching items; the table has 15 assumed rows and the delete runs 0.0003 times per second, far below the 1,000 WCU/s and 3,000 RCU/s partition limits, so no shard suffix is used. The index is KEYS_ONLY because the delete needs only the table key. The status update rewrites the index entry, which adds one index write per status change.

trade_offs.description: The unfiltered read of query `-7865273` (all llm_models rows) becomes a Query on the AllModels GSI, whose partition key is a constant attribute catalog = 'all'.
trade_offs.impact: All 10 models sit in one index partition, which is safe at 0.0002 requests per second and 1,025-byte items; the index projects display_name and the key id, so no base-table read is needed. The index grows only with the number of models, and it would need a shard suffix if the model count reached the thousands.

trade_offs.description: The three embedding tables are keyed on model_id with a composite string sort key (strategy id plus the fragment, post or topic id), so deleting all embeddings of a model (queries `-1435330` , `52403906` and `49917681`) is a Query on the partition and a batch delete, not a Scan.
trade_offs.impact: A model with many embeddings puts all its items under one partition key value: at 590-byte items the 1 MB Query page holds about 1,700 items, and a partition value is limited to 1,000 WCU/s, so a large model's delete runs as repeated batches over time. The halfvec embeddings column is stored as binary; DynamoDB cannot run vector similarity search on it, and no in-scope query does.

trade_offs.description: The lookup of query `-7096413` (post_type = x AND category_id IN up to 8 values) is one Query per category id, on a table keyed by category_id with the sort key post_type#group_id.
trade_offs.impact: The application sends up to 8 Query requests instead of one IN statement; each is a single-partition read. The source unique index (category_id, group_id, post_type) is the key itself, so uniqueness is enforced by the primary key.

trade_offs.description: theme_svg_sprites is keyed on theme_id and user_uploads on user_id plus upload_id, the columns of their unique source indexes (all NOT NULL) and of queries `28794562` and `-2937927`; the surrogate id stays as an attribute.
trade_offs.impact: Both lookups are GetItem calls. A theme_id or upload pair never changes after insert, so the key is stable; reading either table by the source id needs a new index. The sprite bytea column stays inline at an average item size of 345 bytes against the 400 KB item limit.

trade_offs.description: Row counts for all ten tables are assumed from table size over item size (19, 19, 19, 0, 15, 31, 10, 0, 30 and 46 items).
trade_offs.impact: Capacity and cost figures rest on these derived counts; every table is far below any partition limit at the measured rates.

trade_offs.description: shared_drafts, anonymous_users, category_settings and topic_search_data are keyed on the natural column their queries use (topic_id, master_user_id, category_id, topic_id) instead of the generated id.
trade_offs.impact: Each of these columns is unique and NOT NULL in the source (a unique index on it), so a PutItem on the key cannot silently overwrite another row. The generated id stays as an attribute. The key cannot be updated in place: a change is a delete and a put of the item.

trade_offs.description: bookmarks is keyed on user_id plus a composite sort key bookmarkable_key (bookmarkable_type#bookmarkable_id), which mirrors the source unique index on user_id, bookmarkable_type and bookmarkable_id.
trade_offs.impact: The key itself enforces the one-bookmark-per-target rule, so no sentinel item is needed. The source columns bookmarkable_type and bookmarkable_id are nullable, and a row with either NULL has no bookmarkable_key; the migration loads such rows only after a value is supplied. No in-scope write inserts bookmarks.

trade_offs.description: Joins and subqueries become several requests: the allowed_pm_users read (query `4829209`) resolves usernames with a BatchGetItem on the users table that group 1 owns, and the tag_users read (query `5481939`) takes the topic's tag ids from topic_tags, which group 2 owns, before a BatchGetItem on tag_users.
trade_offs.impact: Each read costs one extra request per call and the application picks the highest notification_level and applies the IN filter on notification_level. The extra reads depend on the key schemas the owning groups choose for users and topic_tags. The rates are 0.056 and 0.0041 requests per second.

trade_offs.description: user_fields has 14 items and two reads that name no column (queries `2453444` and `3003621`), so all items share one partition key value (user_field_scope = ALL) and the reads are a Query on it.
trade_offs.impact: The reads total 0.0564 requests per second against 14 items of 754 bytes, far below the 3,000 RCU/s partition limit, so the constant key carries no hot-partition risk. The application sorts the result by position because the sort key is the field id.

trade_offs.description: The tsvector column search_data of topic_search_data and user_search_data is not stored; the items hold raw_data, locale and version.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB has no tsvector type and no full-text matching. The two upserts (queries `3418258` and `7683692`) write the raw text, and full-text search runs on Aurora PostgreSQL, which absorbed the search workload. The row sizes are 1,555 bytes (topics) and 2,176 bytes (users) against the 400 KB item limit, so raw_data stays inline.

trade_offs.description: The orphan clean-up of topic_search_data (query `1857846`) becomes a DeleteItem by topic_id issued by a DynamoDB Streams consumer on the topics table, instead of an anti-join sweep.
trade_offs.impact: The consumer deletes the search item when a topic is removed or its deleted_at passes the retention date. The delete runs after the topic write, which the topics owner (group 5) emits on its stream, and the search item can outlive the topic by the stream delivery delay, normally under one second; the application treats a search item without a live topic as absent.

trade_offs.description: The delete of all given_daily_likes rows of a user (query `8559713`) is a Query on the user_id partition key followed by BatchWriteItem deletes of the returned keys, in batches of 25.
trade_offs.impact: The write is not atomic across batches; a retry of the same delete completes it. given_daily_likes has one item per user and day, so a user holds as many items as days with a like.

trade_offs.description: Row counts for allowed_pm_users, anonymous_users, do_not_disturb_timings, given_daily_likes, shared_drafts, tag_users, bookmarks, category_settings and user_fields are assumed in the design metrics; the source collection has no count for them.
trade_offs.impact: Item counts in the table definitions rest on that assumption (a count of 0 stands for a table whose collected size is under 0.1 MB). Read rates are rounded up to one item for patterns whose collected average rows returned is 0.

trade_offs.description: The do_not_disturb_timings check (query `8338762`) is a Query on user_id with a FilterExpression on starts_at and ends_at, because the table has no sort key on the timestamps.
trade_offs.impact: The filter does not reduce read units: every timing item of the user is read. A user holds a handful of timings, so the read stays under one 4 KB unit.

trade_offs.description: The api_keys item is 724 bytes by its schema while the collected table size divides to 73,400 bytes for its single row.
trade_offs.impact: The item size in the design uses the 724-byte schema figure; the collected size reflects table overhead for a one-row table. The 400 KB item limit is not approached.

trade_offs.description: scheduler_stats is keyed on an application-generated numeric id, and its retention delete (query `5139002051034385017`) becomes DynamoDB Time to Live on an expires_at epoch-seconds attribute instead of a set-based DELETE.
trade_offs.impact: The source database generated the id; the application now generates it before PutItem. TTL removes expired items in the background, within days of expiry and at no write cost; a read that must not see an expired run filters on expires_at. The retention period is added to started_at when the item is written.

trade_offs.description: problem_check_trackers is keyed on the natural pair identifier (partition key) and target (sort key) instead of the surrogate id; the pair is unique in the source (index on identifier and target) and both columns are NOT NULL.
trade_offs.impact: Lookups by identifier and target are a GetItem. The update `4578670901435518703` that the source addresses by id is an UpdateItem on identifier and target, which the caller holds from its earlier read. The id stays as an attribute. Changing identifier or target is a delete and a put.

trade_offs.description: The target-not-equal read (query `3757647435148076712`) is a Query on the identifier partition with a FilterExpression on target.
trade_offs.impact: A filter does not reduce read units; with 13 items in the table (item size 532 bytes) the read cost is one item collection read per request.

trade_offs.description: post_custom_fields and category_custom_fields use the owning entity id as partition key and the source id as numeric sort key; name IN filters are FilterExpressions on the Query.
trade_offs.impact: The sort key returns items in id order, which replaces ORDER BY id. A category read with 7 category ids and 10 names (query `-4224723110330385651`) is 7 Query requests issued by the application. The source ordered-scan concern does not apply because every read carries the partition key.

trade_offs.description: The insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (query `-3970536631062481956`) is a PutItem with attribute_not_exists(id). The source has unique indexes on post_id whose predicates were not collected, so the one-per-post rule for specific names is not enforced by a sentinel item.
trade_offs.impact: A repeated put of the same id is rejected without error to the caller. Duplicates under the same post_id and name that the source blocked through its partial unique indexes are prevented only by the application until the predicates are confirmed and a sentinel item per post and name is added in a TransactWriteItems. The table holds 104 items at 544 bytes.

trade_offs.description: CategoriesByNameValue indexes category_custom_fields on name and value to serve the lookup of category ids by custom field (query `-3475673447205582643`); it projects keys only.
trade_offs.impact: The lookup reads the index and returns category_id, a table key attribute, so no base-table fetch happens. Items with a null value are not indexed. The index lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; no query in this group needs a strongly consistent read of it. A value longer than 2048 bytes cannot be an index key, and each write to name or value costs an extra index write.

trade_offs.description: topic_timers is keyed on timerable_id (partition) and id (sort); type, public_type, status_type and deleted_at are filter conditions, and a sparse index DueTimersByType (active_type, execute_at, id) serves the due and first-by-type reads (queries `7867144291288177551`, `7551743092387284843`).
trade_offs.impact: active_type exists only while deleted_at is null, so soft-deleted timers drop out of the index. The index groups all timers of one type under a few partition key values; at 0.09 requests per second and 13 items this stays far below the partition limits. Results of the first-by-type read arrive in execute_at order and the application orders them by id. The table row count is derived from its size; topic_timers_topic_id_readonly becomes an application rule.

trade_offs.description: problem_check_trackers.details (average row 4033 bytes in the source, 13 rows) and text value columns stay inline in the items.
trade_offs.impact: The average source row of 4033 bytes is 1% of the 400 KB item limit, so no value moves to S3. category_custom_fields has an assumed row count of 38 derived from its size over the schema item size.

trade_offs.description: Context for other groups: this group owns category_custom_fields, post_custom_fields, problem_check_trackers, scheduler_stats and topic_timers; no context tables are used.
trade_offs.impact: No placeholder tables are defined and no table in this group is written by another group.

trade_offs.description: Source tables badge_types, color_schemes and topic_custom_fields keep the source id as the item identity; topic_custom_fields keys on topic_id with the id as sort key, because a topic can hold several rows under one name (only some indexes on (topic_id, name) are unique).
trade_offs.impact: Lookups by id (queries `41950144`, `-3852732`) are GetItem calls and reads of a topic's fields (queries `69327534`, `-6814162`) are Queries on one partition in id order, as the source returns them. The name filter on the multi-name read is applied after the read, so the read bills every field of the topic (19 rows in the whole table).

trade_offs.description: plugin_store_rows keys on (plugin_name, key) and translation_overrides on (locale, translation_key) instead of the surrogate id: each pair is a unique index on NOT NULL columns and is the only way the queries look the rows up.
trade_offs.impact: Lookups are GetItem on the full natural key. A key cannot be updated in place: renaming a plugin key or a translation key is a delete and a put. The id stays as a plain attribute. Both tables hold at most 37 rows each, so the low number of distinct partition values carries no load risk at under 0.1 requests per second.

trade_offs.description: topic_voting_topic_vote_count keeps the generated id as the table key and serves topic_id lookups through the VotesByTopic index, because topic_id is nullable in the source and so does not qualify as a key.
trade_offs.impact: The reads of queries `-6009241` and `-8991302` (the latter a pattern of 30 statements with up to five topic ids) become one Query per topic on the index, replacing the IN list. The index is eventually consistent: it reflects a vote count write once DynamoDB applies the write to it, and a read that needs the latest value reads the base item by id with a strongly consistent GetItem. The table has no in-scope writes and its row count (0) is an assumption from its data size.

trade_offs.description: watched_words keys on action with id as sort key, replacing the source's non-unique lookup by action; the action values are few and the table holds 24 rows.
trade_offs.impact: Queries `32923337` and `78658263` are Queries on one action partition. All words of an action share one partition, which at 0.25 existence checks per second and a few read units per call stays far under the 3,000 RCU/s partition limit; the existence check reads one item with Limit 1.

trade_offs.description: schema_migrations uses a constant partition key migration_set with version as sort key, because the full ordered read (query `31790646`) has no key value to address.
trade_offs.impact: The ordered read of all 2,244 to 2,284 versions is a paginated Query on one partition (about 199 KB at 87 bytes per item, one page). The partition receives 0.026 writes per second and 0.0007 reads per second, far below the 1,000 WCU/s and 3,000 RCU/s limits. The insert (query `26803139`) carries attribute_not_exists(version), matching the source primary key.

trade_offs.description: The retention delete on skipped_email_logs (query `-5145007`) is served by Time to Live on a new expires_at attribute (created_at plus the retention period, in epoch seconds) instead of a DELETE by created_at.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB removes expired items in the background at no write cost, normally within days of expiry, so a read that must not see an expired log filters on expires_at. The retention period is the customer's current cut-off value and is set in the migration. The id is generated by the application (the source sequence is not kept); the insert (query `55175306`) carries attribute_not_exists(id).

trade_offs.description: user_notification_schedules keys on user_id with id as sort key and adds the EnabledSchedules index on a numeric enabled_flag (1 or 0) for the read of query `-6710918`.
trade_offs.impact: The index partition key has two values, which is a hot-key shape in principle; at 0.0002 reads per second and a table of 0 rows (assumed from its data size) the load is far below the limits. If the enabled set grows large, the index key needs a shard suffix. The index mirrors every change of the enabled flag as a delete and put on the index.

trade_offs.description: The row counts of badge_types, color_schemes, plugin_store_rows, skipped_email_logs, topic_custom_fields, topic_voting_topic_vote_count, translation_overrides, user_notification_schedules and watched_words are derived from each table's data size over its item size; schema_migrations uses the collected estimate.
trade_offs.impact: Item counts and storage figures for these tables are approximate. The largest item, user_notification_schedules at 1,047 bytes, and the largest value column (topic_custom_fields.value, plugin_store_rows.value and translation_overrides.original_translation, all TEXT counted at their 1 KB cap) stay inline: average items are 87 to 1,047 bytes against the 400 KB item limit.

trade_offs.description: Retention deletes of `search_logs` (query `3022359a`) and `unsubscribe_keys` (query `9113575a`) are served by Time to Live on an `expires_at` epoch-seconds attribute instead of a scheduled DELETE.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB removes expired items in the background at no write cost, within days of expiry rather than at the cut-off second. Expired items stay readable until then, and any read that must not see them filters on `expires_at`. The retention period is the cut-off the source job passes to its DELETE; the migration computes `expires_at` from `created_at` plus that period.

trade_offs.description: `user_passwords` is keyed on `user_id` instead of the surrogate `id`. `user_id` is unique and not null in the source (14 rows), so the unique constraint is enforced by `attribute_not_exists(user_id)` on the PutItem and needs no sentinel item.
trade_offs.impact: The user lookup (query `8450912a`, 0.0568 requests per second) is a GetItem. The delete by `id` (query `5476648a`, 0.0006 requests per second) deletes by `user_id`; a caller that has only the id reads `user_id` from the `PasswordsById` index first, which lags the base table until DynamoDB applies the write. `user_id` is a user's identity and does not change.

trade_offs.description: `upcoming_change_events` is keyed on the source's unique pair `upcoming_change_name` and `event_type` (both not null) instead of the surrogate `id`; the `EventsByType` index keyed on `event_type` and `created_at` serves the ordered listing.
trade_offs.impact: The IN-list read (query `3093312a`, up to 12 names) is a BatchGetItem and the application sorts its few results by `created_at`, since BatchGetItem returns no order. The insert (query `1621933a`) uses `attribute_not_exists(upcoming_change_name)` for the unique constraint. `event_type` has few distinct values, so `EventsByType` has few partitions; its 0.0137 requests per second on 49 items stays far under the partition limits.

trade_offs.description: The all-rows job name list of `onceoff_logs` (query `-7989811`) and the job name existence check (query `1472164a`) run on the `OnceoffByScope` index whose partition key is the constant `log_scope` = ONCEOFF and whose sort key is `job_name`.
trade_offs.impact: The table has 91 rows, so one partition holds the whole index and carries 0.0095 read units per second, far below the 3,000 limit. This replaces a full-table read with a Query. `job_name` is not unique in the source, so the base key stays the surrogate `id`, generated by the application.

trade_offs.description: The IS NOT NULL and boolean tests on `theme_modifier_sets` (queries `PAT-16` members and `5076669a`) cannot be filters on GetItem, so the application reads the item by `theme_id` and tests the attribute.
trade_offs.impact: Each read returns the full 572-byte item, one read unit of 0.5 at most; no index is added. `theme_id` is unique and not null in the source, so it is the key. An empty array column is omitted from the item because DynamoDB sets cannot be empty.

trade_offs.description: The INSERT ... SELECT of `web_hook_event_types_hooks` (query `2584108a`) becomes a Query on one `web_hook_event_type_id` partition followed by a BatchWriteItem of the copied items under the target event type.
trade_offs.impact: The copy is no longer one atomic statement: each BatchWriteItem takes at most 25 items, and a failed batch is retried by the application. The table currently holds no rows (row count assumed), so the copy is small.

trade_offs.description: Ids that PostgreSQL sequences generated (`search_logs.id`, `onceoff_logs.id`, `upcoming_change_events.id`, `user_passwords.id`) are generated by the application, and PutItem carries `attribute_not_exists` on the key.
trade_offs.impact: The source's INSERT ... RETURNING id is replaced by an id the application creates before the write. `search_logs` stays keyed on `id` because no query reads it by another column; `search_logs` item size is 1530 bytes against the 400 KB limit, and `user_agent` stays inline.

trade_offs.description: Row counts of `onceoff_logs`, `theme_modifier_sets`, `upcoming_change_events` and `web_hook_event_types` are derived from each table's size over its item size.
trade_offs.impact: Item counts and index sizes for these tables are estimates; at 91, 37, 49 and 130 items they do not change any key choice.

trade_offs.description: The table is keyed on the natural attribute `name` instead of the surrogate `id`.
trade_offs.impact: Reads, deletes and renames of site settings (queries `856517717`-style lookups, `4961560a`, `3228630`, `5564386`) address a setting by name, so they are single-item operations. `name` is the source's unique, NOT NULL index with 27 distinct values for 27 rows. A DynamoDB key cannot be updated in place, so a rename (queries `5564386` and `8807180`, about 5 per hour) becomes a delete of the old item and a put of the new one in one TransactWriteItems of 2 items, with `attribute_not_exists(name)` on the put that keeps names unique. The id stays reachable through the SettingsById index.

trade_offs.description: Update by id (query `18968104`) uses the SettingsById index, which holds the keys only.
trade_offs.impact: The update runs a Query on SettingsById to find the name and then an UpdateItem on the base table. The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; the update reads the name from a freshly renamed setting only after that write is applied, and a missing item makes the `attribute_exists(name)` condition fail the update. The index is read about 0.0004 times per second, so KEYS_ONLY avoids projecting attributes that every write would copy.

trade_offs.description: The full-table read (query `-5236333`) is a Query on the AllSettings index, whose partition key is the constant `settings_scope` = `ALL`.
trade_offs.impact: The table holds 27 items, so one partition key value holds the whole index; at 0.0014 reads per second the load is far below the 3,000 RCU/s limit for one key value. Each write to the table also writes the AllSettings index, which the cost check counts. The read returns name, data_type and value from the INCLUDE projection and needs no base-table fetch. The index lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a caller that must see its own write reads the item by name with a strongly consistent GetItem.

trade_offs.description: The id column was generated by a database sequence; the application now generates it.
trade_offs.impact: Inserts (query `-3992283`) and copies (query `4188825`) write an application-generated numeric id, since the table key is the name and the id is an attribute. Uniqueness of the id is not enforced by DynamoDB; the SettingsById index does not enforce it either, so the application takes the next id from a counter or a UUID-derived number.

trade_offs.description: Name uniqueness is enforced by the table key and a conditional write; no sentinel item is needed.
trade_offs.impact: Insert, copy and rename put the item with `attribute_not_exists(name)`, so a taken name cancels the write. Query `8807180` (rename only when the new name is free) uses the same condition inside its 2-item TransactWriteItems, which costs 4 write units per KB of item (prepare and commit for each item). The copy (query `4188825`) is a GetItem of the source name followed by a conditional PutItem, not an INSERT ... SELECT.

trade_offs.description: The `value` text column stays inline.
