trade_offs.impact: The table's `avg_row_size_bytes` is 1942 against the 400 KB item limit, so settings are stored as one item each with no S3 offload. All 27 items together are about 52 KB.

trade_offs.description: topic_users is keyed by topic_id (partition) and user_id (sort) instead of the surrogate id, and the id is kept as a plain attribute.
trade_offs.impact: The source's unique index on (topic_id, user_id) becomes the table key, so a conditional PutItem rejects a duplicate and no sentinel item is needed; the 726-row table holds one item collection per topic. Every lookup in this group (queries `2857022` and its siblings) names both columns, so the id is never a lookup key. Lookups by the surrogate id alone are not served; the id is generated by the application when it was generated by the database sequence.

trade_offs.description: The IN-list reads of one user across topics become one BatchGetItem of (topic_id, user_id) keys; the existence checks and the topic read become Query calls with a FilterExpression.
trade_offs.impact: A filter does not reduce the read units a Query consumes, which is one item of 881 bytes (0.5 read unit eventually consistent) per call here. A BatchGetItem takes at most 100 keys and 16 MB per call, so longer lists are split. Query `-2081487` filters last_read_post_number on the topic partition; a topic with many readers reads every item of its partition on each call.

trade_offs.description: TopicUsersByUser (partition user_id, sort topic_id, INCLUDE notifications_reason_id and total_msecs_viewed) serves the two key-scoped writes on topic_users by user_id.
trade_offs.impact: Query `931558391` reads the user's rows from the index, filters notifications_reason_id absent and updates notification_level per row; query `-5857369` reads the keys and deletes them in batches of 25. Neither is a Scan. The index is eventually consistent and lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a sweep that must see a row written a moment earlier reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem. Every write to topic_users also writes the index, doubling its write units; at 0.0817 updates per second this is below 0.2 write units per second and the index key attributes never change, so updates of other attributes do not rewrite it.

trade_offs.description: The set-based CASE update (query `931558391`) becomes a per-row UpdateItem: the application computes notification_level from the projected total_msecs_viewed.
trade_offs.impact: The source updates all matching rows in one statement. DynamoDB has no set-based update, so each row is one UpdateItem; the 4.92 rows per user seen on the matching delete (query `-5857369`) put the batch well under the 100-item transaction limit, but the sweep is not atomic across rows and a failed run is retried for the rows still lacking a reason.

trade_offs.description: reviewables is keyed by id with five global secondary indexes: ReviewablesByTopic, ReviewablesByStatusScore, ReviewablesByStatusCreated, ReviewablesByTarget and ReviewablesByCreator.
trade_offs.impact: The table has 9 rows (the source has no row count; the figure is derived from the table's size of 0.08 MB over the 1111-byte item), so the indexes cost little to hold, but each insert or status change writes up to five index entries. The type and target_id pair is unique in the source, but target_id is nullable, so it is not a safe key and no write in this group inserts reviewables; no sentinel is written. ReviewablesByTarget and ReviewablesByTopic are sparse on target_id and topic_id: rows without the attribute are not indexed.

trade_offs.description: ReviewablesByStatusScore and ReviewablesByStatusCreated use the low-cardinality status as partition key.
trade_offs.impact: All items of one status share a partition. The table holds 9 items and these patterns total 0.0127 requests per second, far below the 3,000 read and 1,000 write units per second of a partition, so no shard suffix is added. If the table grows to millions of items in one status, the status partition would need a shard suffix and a query over every shard.

trade_offs.description: The count in query `1175638` is a Query on ReviewablesByStatusScore with Select=COUNT, and the ORDER BY id reads (queries `2643383` and `5026464`) are ordered by score or created_at in the index.
trade_offs.impact: The count reads and bills every item of the status and score range (1 MB per page, summed); at 9 items and 0.0002 requests per second no counter item is kept. Query `2643383` sorts its ids descending in the application. Query `5026464` returns the oldest rows by created_at rather than by id; with ids that grow with time the two orders agree, and a batch limit applies to the created_at order.

trade_offs.description: The delete of reviewables by created_by_id (query `-7092816`) is a Query on ReviewablesByCreator (KEYS_ONLY) followed by BatchWriteItem deletes by id.
trade_offs.impact: The source deletes in one statement; DynamoDB deletes in batches of 25 items with no atomicity across batches, and each delete also removes the row's entries from the other four indexes. A rerun deletes the rows that remain.

trade_offs.description: Timestamps are stored as ISO 8601 strings, the JSON payload as a map, and the sequence ids as application-generated numbers.
trade_offs.impact: ISO 8601 strings sort in time order, which the created_at range reads rely on. The payload column has no declared size limit; the table's average item is 1111 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, so payload stays inline. Applications generate reviewables.id and topic_users.id since DynamoDB has no sequence.

trade_offs.description: The AI agent name is unique in the source (`index_ai_agents_on_name`) and query `7964039920894090174` inserts it, so the insert is one TransactWriteItems of 2 items: the agent in `ai_agents` and a name sentinel in `ai_agent_names`, each Put with attribute_not_exists.
trade_offs.impact: A duplicate name cancels the whole insert instead of overwriting another agent. The transaction costs 2 writes per item (prepare and commit), about 10 write units per insert at 0.0003 inserts per second; the 2-item size is far below the 100-item limit.

trade_offs.description: `ai_agents` keeps the source id as the partition key because query `-9107418073878310695` reads by id; `system_prompt` and `description` stay inline in the item, whose measured average is 3755 bytes against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: The table counts both columns at the 1 KB cap, so one stored prompt can approach 400 KB; a prompt that reaches that size moves to S3 with a pointer attribute. The surrogate id is application-generated instead of a database sequence.

trade_offs.description: `sitemaps` and `application_requests` and `web_crawler_requests` are keyed on their natural unique keys (sitemaps.name; date with req_type; date with user_agent), which are unique, NOT NULL and stable, instead of the generated id.
trade_offs.impact: Queries `-8729198876356079750`, `6668674146221133871` and `7106625407976767713` become GetItem or UpdateItem on the full key with no index. The user_agent sort key must stay under the 1024-byte sort key limit. The source id is kept as a plain attribute where a query returns it.

trade_offs.description: The upsert in query `6668674146221133871` (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET count = count + excluded.count) becomes UpdateItem with ADD count on the date and req_type key.
trade_offs.impact: The increment is atomic and creates the item when it is absent, so no condition or read-before-write is needed. All request types of one day share a partition key value, at 0.2 write units per second against the 1000 limit.

trade_offs.description: The full read of `embeddable_hosts` (query `5571699630796892942`) is served by giving all 22 rows the constant partition key value scope=embeddable_hosts, so it is one Query on one item collection instead of a Scan.
trade_offs.impact: The read costs about 3 four-KB read pages per call at 0.02 calls per second. A write to this table must set the constant scope attribute on every item.

trade_offs.description: Queries `2931539718557711172` and `1217360975432785261` (redesign requirements) are served by GSIs `EmbedsByTopic` (topic_id, INCLUDE deleted_at) and `DirectoryColumnsByName` (name, with type as sort key, ALL), with the IS NULL conditions on deleted_at and icon applied as attribute_not_exists filters.
trade_offs.impact: Both indexes are eventually consistent: a new row appears in the index after DynamoDB applies the write, and a read that must see the latest write uses the base table item. The filters discard rows after they are read, which is bounded by 7 and 45 rows in the two tables.

trade_offs.description: Query `-5195588254230218940` (action_type with last_match_at before a cutoff, or created_at before it when last_match_at is NULL) is served by GSI `ScreenedByActionAndMatch` on action_type and a derived match_sort_at that holds last_match_at, or created_at when it is NULL.
trade_offs.impact: match_sort_at is written with every item and rewritten whenever last_match_at changes, so each such update also rewrites the index entry. action_type has few values, but the table holds 50 rows at 0.0002 reads per second, so one partition key value carries a negligible load.

trade_offs.description: Filters on non-key columns (method and enabled in query `763652916241229345`, change_state in `-2135502268557629957`, revoked_at in `7661205089442229807`) run as FilterExpressions on a Query by user_id.
trade_offs.impact: A filter does not reduce the read capacity consumed, which is the items of one user: 15 to 27 rows in these tables across all users, so the extra read cost is below one 4 KB unit per call.

trade_offs.description: `user_associated_accounts` keeps the source id as the partition key and serves query `-7832492340302674463` through GSI `AccountByProviderUser` on provider_name and user_id, because user_id is nullable and the key must not depend on it.
trade_offs.impact: The index is eventually consistent. Its unique constraints are not enforced because no in-scope write inserts or changes these rows; the other unique indexes of the group's tables (client_id, key_hash, auth_token, embed_url, ip_address) also have no in-scope insert and need no sentinel.

trade_offs.description: Generated ids of `post_stats`, `schema_migration_details` and `color_scheme_colors` are produced by the application, and their inserts (queries `5423936073563966392`, `-4917791749421847216`, `-8362095136812523352`) carry attribute_not_exists(id).
trade_offs.impact: The database sequence is gone; the application needs a unique id generator, and the condition makes an id collision fail instead of overwriting a row.

trade_offs.description: The row counts of 12 tables in this group are derived from table size over item size because the source has no count.
trade_offs.impact: Item counts and the capacity figures that rest on them are estimates until the migration counts the rows.

trade_offs.description: Tables whose queries all look rows up by user_id (category_users, dismissed_topic_users, draft_sequences, drafts, user_security_keys, user_visits) use user_id as the partition key with the second lookup column as the sort key instead of the generated id.
trade_offs.impact: Each (user, second column) pair is unique in the source (unique indexes on category_users, dismissed_topic_users, draft_sequences, drafts and user_visits), so a PutItem cannot overwrite a different row. The generated id stays as a plain attribute and is not a lookup key; a caller that reads these rows by id alone needs a new index. dismissed_topic_users has nullable user_id and topic_id in the source, so rows with a null in either column cannot be keyed and are rejected by the migration.

trade_offs.description: discourse_solved_solved_topics is keyed on topic_id, which the source defines as unique and not null, and the table has no secondary index.
trade_offs.impact: Both solved-topic reads address a topic id, so GetItem and BatchGetItem serve them directly. The source's unique answer_post_id and the generated id are stored as attributes with no index because no in-scope query reads by them. No in-scope write sets them.

trade_offs.description: The IN-list reads on discourse_solved_solved_topics (up to 5 topic ids) and dismissed_topic_users (up to 5 topic ids for one user) become one BatchGetItem each.
trade_offs.impact: A BatchGetItem bills one read per key, whether or not the item exists, so each call costs 5 keys at 0.5 read unit each (eventually consistent). The application handles any unprocessed keys the response returns by retrying them.

trade_offs.description: The category notification query that joins topics through a subquery is split into two reads: the application first reads the topic's category_id from the topics table, which group 5 designs, then runs GetItem on category_users with the notification_level filter applied in the application.
trade_offs.impact: The pair of reads is not atomic: a topic moved to another category between them returns the level of the old category. The window is the time between the two calls, and the application re-reads the topic when it needs a consistent answer. This group defines no topics table and writes none.

trade_offs.description: user_security_keys uses the sort key factor_created_id = factor_type#created_at#id so one Query by user and factor_type returns the keys in created_at order; the enabled check is a filter on that Query.
trade_offs.impact: The filter runs on a user's own item collection only (13 keys in the whole table, avg_row_size_bytes 784), so the filter reads cost no more than the item collection already holds. A change to factor_type or created_at changes the sort key and is a delete plus a put. credential_id is unique in the source but no in-scope write sets it, so it needs no sentinel.

trade_offs.description: The deletes by user_id on user_security_keys, user_visits, drafts and draft_sequences run as a Query on the partition key followed by BatchWriteItem deletes of 25 keys per call.
trade_offs.impact: The delete is not one atomic statement: a failure part-way leaves some rows deleted, and the application retries the remaining keys, which is safe because deletes are idempotent. Each deleted item costs one write unit per 1 KB. user_id has no collected cardinality, so the per-user item count is unknown; a user's visit rows grow by one item per day active.

trade_offs.description: The visit count on user_visits is a Query with Select=COUNT on user_id and a visited_at range, with posts_read as a filter, with no counter item.
trade_offs.impact: The Query reads and bills every item in the date range before the filter applies (295 bytes per item, 1 MB per page). The pattern runs about once an hour, so a maintained counter would cost more writes than it saves reads. Because user_id has no collected cardinality, a user with many visit rows pays for each one per call.

trade_offs.description: javascript_caches is an item collection holding the cache record plus two sentinel items: THEME#{theme_id} and THEMEFIELD#{theme_field_id}#{name}.
trade_offs.impact: The source enforces unique theme_id and unique (theme_field_id, name), and the insert writes both. The insert becomes one TransactWriteItems of up to 3 items (1 + 2 unique attributes), each Put guarded by attribute_not_exists(cache_pk), so a taken value cancels the insert. A sentinel is written only when its value is not null. Each item costs 2 write units per 1 KB (prepare and commit), a canceled transaction included. The lookup by theme_id is a GetItem on the sentinel and a GetItem on the record. Rows with a null theme_id are reachable by (theme_field_id, name) only.

trade_offs.description: The javascript_caches id is generated by the application when it writes the record item, replacing the database sequence that returned it.
trade_offs.impact: The application supplies a unique numeric id (for example from a time-ordered generator) before the transaction, since the sentinels hold it. The insert no longer returns a generated value.

trade_offs.description: polls is keyed on post_id with the poll id as sort key, and the unique (post_id, name) index has no sentinel because no in-scope write inserts or changes polls.
trade_offs.impact: One Query on post_id serves both poll reads and returns polls in id order. The source allows a null post_id; those rows cannot be keyed by post and are not migrated into this table. The row count (11) is assumed from the table's data size.

trade_offs.description: drafts.data (TEXT) stays inline in the drafts item; the sequence comparison of the revisions lookup runs in the application.
trade_offs.impact: The table's avg_row_size_bytes is 514 against the 400 KB item limit, so inline storage fits. The GetItem returns revisions and sequence, and the caller treats a sequence mismatch as no match, matching the source's WHERE clause.

trade_offs.description: Row counts for category_users, discourse_solved_solved_topics, dismissed_topic_users, draft_sequences, drafts, polls, user_security_keys and user_visits are derived from each table's data size, as the source has no count for them.
trade_offs.impact: Item counts and storage figures for these tables are approximations; the traffic is far below any partition limit, so the design does not depend on them.

trade_offs.description: Each of the six tables keeps the source's access key: categories, themes and user_profiles are keyed on their id or user_id, optimized_images on upload_id with a width, height and extension sort key, and sidebar_section_links on user_id with a link type and id sort key.
trade_offs.impact: Every lookup the queries make is a GetItem or Query on the base key. The composite keys of optimized_images and sidebar_section_links are the source's unique indexes, so a duplicate insert is rejected by the key itself. The surrogate id of those two tables stays as an attribute, and optimized_images keeps it reachable through a GSI.

trade_offs.description: optimized_images is keyed on the natural unique index (upload_id, width, height, extension) and the OptimizedImagesById GSI serves the update by id (query `-9291540`); ids are generated by the application instead of the sequence.
trade_offs.impact: The lookups (`70624213`, `6635859`) are single-partition reads at about 0.0009 requests per second. The update by id finds the table key through an eventually consistent GSI read, which can lag a just-inserted image until DynamoDB applies the write to the index; the application reads the base item when it needs the latest write.

trade_offs.description: The visibility check (query `83441274`) is split across tables: a GetItem on categories, a Query on category_groups by category_id, and a lookup of the user's groups in group_users, which design group 9 owns; no placeholder for group_users is defined here.
trade_offs.impact: The three reads run as separate requests in the application instead of one SQL statement with subqueries, at 0.0641 requests per second. The group membership read depends on the group_users design of the owning group.

trade_offs.description: The query `-6956980` that selects every theme id is served by the ThemeIds GSI, whose partition key is the constant attribute theme_scope, instead of a Scan.
trade_offs.impact: All 35 theme items sit in one index partition. The read rate is 0.0004 requests per second and theme writes are rare, so the index stays far below the 1,000 WCU/s and 3,000 RCU/s partition limits.

trade_offs.description: The consistency repair sweep (query `2539559289`) is modelled as a write-time rule plus a safety-net sweep over the ProfilesByGrantedTitleBadge GSI, which only holds profiles that carry granted_title_badge_id (the share without it is not collected; the index is sized at all 53 profiles).
trade_offs.impact: The write that changes a user's title also clears the badge on the profile; the sweep Queries the index, checks each user's title in the users table owned by design group 1, and sends one conditional UpdateItem per profile. No Scan and no set-based UPDATE ... FROM join is used. The index adds one extra write per insert or badge change on user_profiles.

trade_offs.description: SidebarLinksBySection projects ALL attributes, and the delete by user (query `77715457`) runs as a Query on the user partition followed by BatchWriteItem deletes of about three items.
trade_offs.impact: The index serves the 12-row section listing (query `49475884`) at 0.0003 requests per second and each link write is also written to the index. The ALL projection keeps the listing at one request; the delete issues one read and one batch write instead of one SQL DELETE.

trade_offs.description: The sidebar insert (query `-4963619`) uses ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so each of its three links is a PutItem with attribute_not_exists(user_id), not one BatchWriteItem or a transaction.
trade_offs.impact: A link that already exists is skipped and the other links are still written, as in the source. The unique index on (sidebar_section_id, user_id, position) allows several NULL sections and is not written by this insert, so it gets no sentinel item; the unique indexes on categories (email_in, name) and themes (remote_theme_id) have no in-scope writes and need none.

trade_offs.description: Large text columns stay inline: categories has a 3,088-byte schema item (description and topic_template counted at 1 KB each) against the 400 KB item limit, and user_profiles has a 2,722-byte schema item with bio_raw and bio_cooked counted at 1 KB each.
trade_offs.impact: No S3 offload is needed at the measured sizes. categories averages 20,972 bytes per row in the source including index and storage overhead, so an item larger than 400 KB would be rejected by DynamoDB; none is expected for 8 category rows. Row counts for category_groups, optimized_images and themes are derived from the tables' data size.

trade_offs.description: The profile update (query `-4569983`) and optimized image update (query `-9291540`) carry attribute_exists conditions, and the profile insert carries attribute_not_exists(user_id).
trade_offs.impact: An update to a missing item fails instead of creating a partial item, as the source UPDATE matches no row. Each unconditional read after an update can use ReturnValues=ALL_NEW on the UpdateItem.

trade_offs.description: Seventeen small reference and configuration tables each keep their own table, keyed by the column their query filters on, with the source id kept as an attribute or sort key.
trade_offs.impact: Each table holds between 0 and 130 items (row counts are derived from table size, since the source has no counts), so every read is a GetItem or a Query on a partition key and no read is a Scan. A team used to joins now reads each table on its own.

trade_offs.description: developers is keyed on user_id, permalinks on url, custom_emojis and site_setting_groups on name, instead of the generated id. Each is unique in the source (a unique index on a NOT NULL column) and the id stays as an attribute.
trade_offs.impact: The lookups by user_id, url and name are single-item reads with no index. A key cannot be updated in place, so renaming an emoji or a setting group or changing a permalink url is a delete plus a put of the item.

trade_offs.description: group_mentions.post_id and group_id, topic_voting_category_settings.category_id are nullable in the source but are key attributes here.
trade_offs.impact: A source row with a NULL in a key column cannot become an item and is skipped by the migration. The source rows are expected to carry values, because their unique indexes and lookups use these columns.

trade_offs.description: category_required_tag_groups uses the sort key order_tag_group (zero-padded order, then tag_group_id) so the Query returns required tag groups in the source's ORDER BY order and the pair (category_id, tag_group_id) stays unique.
trade_offs.impact: The sort key is derived by the migration and rewritten by the application whenever order changes: a change of order is a delete and a put of the item.

trade_offs.description: The reads of every row of site_setting_groups, topic_voting_category_settings and custom_emojis use a GSI whose partition key is the constant list_key, instead of a Scan.
trade_offs.impact: The three tables hold 37, 0 and 29 items and are read at most 0.0014 times per second, so one partition value carries the whole load far below the 3,000 RCU/s limit. If a table grows past a few thousand items, the constant key becomes a hot key and needs a shard suffix.

trade_offs.description: The deletes on admin_notices (by subject and identifier, filtered on a value in details) and reviewable_histories (by created_by_id) are served by a GSI Query that finds the item keys and a BatchWriteItem that deletes them.
trade_offs.impact: The GSIs lag the table until DynamoDB applies each write to them, so a delete that must remove an item written moments earlier reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem first. The details filter is applied after the read, so the Query reads every item under that subject and identifier, which is a handful of items at 26 rows. The GSI on admin_notices projects details (about 150 bytes per item) to evaluate the filter without a base-table fetch.

trade_offs.description: backup_metadata.id was generated by a database sequence and returned by the insert; the application now generates the id and the Put carries attribute_not_exists(id).
trade_offs.impact: The application owns id generation (for example a UUID-derived number or a time-ordered id) and a collision fails the write instead of overwriting a row. No other unique column is written by an in-scope query, so no sentinel items are needed.

trade_offs.description: The IN-list reads (theme_site_settings with 2 theme ids, sidebar_urls with 12 ids) run as one Query per theme_id and one BatchGetItem for up to 12 ids.
trade_offs.impact: The application issues the requests in parallel and merges the results; the 12 sidebar items of 1,371 bytes each are far below the 16 MB BatchGetItem limit.

trade_offs.description: permalinks averages 2,476 bytes per item and sidebar_urls 1,371 bytes; every other table in this group is under 700 bytes.
trade_offs.impact: All items stay far below the 400 KB item limit, so no column moves to S3.

trade_offs.description: The highest design rate in this group is 0.0198 requests per second, so every table and GSI uses under 0.01 percent of one partition key value's limit.
trade_offs.impact: No hot partition mitigation is needed, and on-demand capacity costs are dominated by the minimum billed unit per request.

trade_offs.description: theme_fields is keyed by its unique index (theme_id, target_id, type_id, name) instead of the generated id: partition key theme_id, sort key field_key = target_id#type_id#name.
trade_offs.impact: Every query in the group filters on theme_id, and the four-column index is unique on NOT NULL columns, so a PutItem with attribute_not_exists(field_key) enforces uniqueness without a sentinel item. The key cannot be updated in place: changing any of the four columns is a delete and a put.

trade_offs.description: The id column is generated by the database sequence in the source; the application now generates it and keeps it as an attribute indexed by the ThemeFieldById GSI.
trade_offs.impact: The update of value_baked by id (query `8669704332297115684`) resolves the table key from the KEYS_ONLY GSI, then runs UpdateItem; the GSI lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it, and a lookup right after an insert reads the base item through the theme_id key instead. The index adds one write unit per insert at 0.0018 inserts per second.

trade_offs.description: Filters on name, type_id and target_id (equality, IN and OR) run as a Query on the theme_id partition with a FilterExpression, not as separate indexes.
trade_offs.impact: A Query bills every item it reads before the filter. A theme holds 155 rows over the whole table, with query `-3578259523147184958` returning 68.9 items on average at 0.0003 requests per second, so the filtered reads at about 0.06 requests per second cost roughly 2 read units per second in total. A GSI per filter would cost more in writes than it saves.

trade_offs.description: The ORDER BY name, id of query `-7649042005127172320` is done by the application; the join to a one-row derived table in query `5946854840824979888` is dropped.
trade_offs.impact: The Query on theme_id and a target_id prefix returns about 12 items, which the application sorts by name. The derived table supplies a constant sort column for one theme_id, so dropping it changes no result.

trade_offs.description: The value and value_baked text columns stay inline in the item; the table's avg_row_size_bytes is 3383 against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: Reads return whole items, billed per 4 KB, so a full-theme read of 68.9 items costs about 29 eventually consistent read units. Moving text to S3 would add a fetch to every read for no size gain.

trade_offs.description: ThemeFieldById projects KEYS_ONLY because it only finds the table key for the update by id.
trade_offs.impact: The index stores about 100 bytes per item and the update reads no non-key attribute from it, so no base-table fetch is added.

trade_offs.description: category_featured_topics is keyed by (category_id, topic_id) and read in rank order through CategoryTopicsByRank, whose partition key is the constant list_key.
trade_offs.impact: Query `6847889062294180867` has no WHERE clause, so a DynamoDB Scan would be the alternative; the index returns the 36 rows in rank order with one Query. All rows share one index partition, which carries 0.0061 reads per second and 0.0771 writes per second at design load, far below the 3,000 read and 1,000 write limits per key value. Query `974806976840491591` deletes by category through a Query on the partition key plus BatchWriteItem.

trade_offs.description: flags keeps the source id as its key and reads all flags in position order through FlagsByPosition, partition key list_key (constant).
trade_offs.impact: Query `3672754895125612752` (ORDER BY position, no key value) becomes one Query over 8 items instead of a Scan. The table holds about 40 items and the index sees 0.0004 reads per second, so one partition carries it. The natural column name_key is nullable and not unique in the source, so it is not used as the key.

trade_offs.description: invites and invited_users share one item collection keyed by invite_id, with entity rows INVITE and INVITEE#{id}; user lookups use the sparse index InviteesByUser (user_id, redeemed_at, KEYS_ONLY) and email lookups use InvitesByEmail (ALL).
trade_offs.impact: Query `-3983690881457160113` joined the two tables; it is now a Query on InviteesByUser followed by a BatchGetItem of the INVITE items, with ordering by invite id and the limit applied by the application. The KEYS_ONLY index adds one base-table read per returned invite, counted in the invites read entry at 0.056 requests per second. Invites without a redeemed_at or without a user_id are not in the index, which is what the redeemed_at filter requires. The source reports 0 returned rows for this query; the design counts 1 invite per call. The invite_key and (user_id, invite_id) unique indexes have no in-scope write, so no sentinel items are created for them.

trade_offs.description: The deleted_at IS NULL test of the email lookups is a FilterExpression attribute_not_exists(deleted_at) on InvitesByEmail; deleted_at is written only for deleted invites.
trade_offs.impact: The filter runs after the read, so the read bills every invite stored under the email; each email holds a handful of invites at the table's 10 items, so the cost is one 4 KB read unit per call.

trade_offs.description: user_custom_fields keeps the unique index on value through a sentinel table user_custom_field_values keyed by value; the (name, user_id) unique index is the base key (user_id, name).
trade_offs.impact: Update `2866689475356927595` runs as a GetItem of the old value's sentinel (strongly consistent), then one TransactWriteItems of 3 items: delete the old sentinel, put the new sentinel with attribute_not_exists(value), and update the record with the condition that value still equals the old value. Each item costs two write units per KB (prepare and commit), including a canceled transaction. A NULL value gets no sentinel. Values are limited to 2,048 bytes as a partition key, so a longer value cannot be stored in the sentinel table. The source index has no recorded predicate, so the design enforces uniqueness on every non-null value.

trade_offs.description: Reads of user_custom_fields use the key (user_id, name): query `-6794419130351561971` is a BatchGetItem of three names and query `7294455028325933846` is a Query on user_id; both drop ORDER BY id.
trade_offs.impact: The application orders the returned items by id. The id column stays as an attribute. The row count (19) is derived from the table size, so these figures rest on that assumption.

trade_offs.description: Ids that the database generated (category_featured_topics.id, user_histories.id and the key of new rows) are generated by the application, and every insert carries attribute_not_exists on its key.
trade_offs.impact: Inserts `-6902067223063288141`, `-5440919867260555248` and `1410136327257395881` fail on a duplicate key instead of overwriting a row. The application owns the id sequence after the move.

trade_offs.description: user_histories has two GSIs: HistoryByActor (acting_user_id, action; KEYS_ONLY) and HistoryByTarget (target_user_id, then action and created_at; INCLUDE previous_value, new_value).
trade_offs.impact: HistoryByActor only finds the base keys for the bulk update, so a KEYS_ONLY index costs the least on the insert path. HistoryByTarget projects the two compared values so the FilterExpression of query `-4634586055388130285` runs inside the index. Each insert writes the base table and both indexes (3 write units at 1 KB). Index reads are eventually consistent: the check reads rows written by an earlier request, and until DynamoDB applies the write to the index a just-written row can be missing from it.

trade_offs.description: The bulk update `6213645647369225488` (details = CONCAT(details, suffix) for one actor and 123 action codes) becomes a Query on HistoryByActor, application filtering of the action codes, and one UpdateItem per id.
trade_offs.impact: No Scan is used and no wide transaction is needed: user_histories holds 81 items, so one actor matches a small number of them. The updates are separate requests, so a failure partway leaves some rows updated; a rerun appends the suffix again to the rows already updated, so the caller tracks which ids it has finished. The 123 action codes exceed the 100-operand limit of a filter expression, so the application filters them.

trade_offs.description: Large-value columns stay inline: user_options is 3,300 bytes per item (schema size; the measured average is 7,490 bytes), user_histories 1,013 bytes (measured 2,330 bytes), invites 1,084 bytes.
trade_offs.impact: All sit far under the 400 KB item limit, and the design counts no capped text column. A user_options read rounds up to one 4 KB read unit; the measured average of 7,490 bytes would cost 2 units, which doubles that pattern's 0.1622 read units per second and stays under 0.01% of the partition limit.

trade_offs.description: Row counts for flags (40), invites (10), invited_users (0) and user_custom_fields (19) are derived from each table's size because the source has no count.
trade_offs.impact: Item counts, index sizes and the capacity figures for these tables rest on that derivation.

trade_offs.description: Array columns (flags.applies_to, user_options.theme_ids, seen_popups) are stored as lists and timestamps as ISO 8601 strings.
trade_offs.impact: A list holds an empty array, which a set type cannot, so theme_ids with its default empty array loads without change. Timestamps sort lexicographically in time order, which the created_at and redeemed_at ranges rely on.

trade_offs.description: The table is keyed by the natural unique key (target, digest) instead of the generated id.
trade_offs.impact: Both columns are NOT NULL and form a unique index in the source, so a lookup by target and digest (query `-493863` pattern PAT-4) is one GetItem and a duplicate insert fails on the conditional PutItem. The id column stays reachable through the StylesheetIdsByTarget index.

trade_offs.description: The id column was a database sequence; the application now generates it as a number, and the id index orders each target's entries by it.
trade_offs.impact: Ids must increase over time for the newest-first read of query `3465310544` and the older-than-id delete of query `-6436268` to keep their order; the application supplies a monotonic value such as a timestamp-based id.

trade_offs.description: StylesheetIdsByTarget projects keys only and serves the newest-first id read and the key lookup for the older-than-id delete.
trade_offs.impact: The index holds 52 items at about 60 bytes each and adds one index write per insert and delete. Reads return only id, which the index holds, so no base-table fetch occurs. The index lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; the delete finds entries written before that point only, which is acceptable for cache cleanup.

trade_offs.description: The retention delete (query `-6072012`) uses Time to Live on an expires_at epoch-seconds attribute set to created_at plus the retention period, instead of a scan with a batch delete.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background within days of expiry at no write cost, so the cut-off is not exact to the second; a read that must not see an expired stylesheet filters on expires_at. The retention period is not in the query telemetry and is set by the application when it writes the item.

trade_offs.description: The content column stays inline in the item. The table's measured average row is 75215 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, while the schema-based item size is 459 bytes because text columns are counted at a fixed size.
trade_offs.impact: Reads and writes are billed on the 75 KB measured size, which is about 19 read units of 4 KB and 74 write units of 1 KB per item; at under 0.01 requests per second this costs less than moving content to S3. An entry that grows toward 400 KB moves content to S3 with a pointer attribute.

trade_offs.description: Target has few distinct values (52 rows in total), so the base table and index partitions each hold a handful of target values.
trade_offs.impact: Total load is under 0.01 units per second, far below the 3,000 read and 1,000 write units per second a key value carries, so no sharding is applied.

trade_offs.description: The table is keyed on token_hash instead of the surrogate id, with a GSI on id.
trade_offs.impact: token_hash is unique in the source (unique index on a NOT NULL column), has 97 distinct values in 97 rows and never changes, so a conditional PutItem enforces its uniqueness without a sentinel item. Lookups by the source id (queries `85658365` and `-8086318`) read the KEYS_ONLY GSI TokensById, then act on the base item by token_hash; the GSI is eventually consistent and lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it.

trade_offs.description: Lookups by email and by user_id plus email are served by the GSIs TokensByEmail and TokensByUser, both projecting ALL attributes.
trade_offs.impact: The source queries return SELECT * and the table is small (avg_row_size_bytes 1405 against the 400 KB item limit), so ALL avoids a base-table fetch; the indexed attributes email and user_id are not updated after insert, so no write amplification arises. The email lookup (query `2741945`) was an unindexed filter in the source and is now a Query. Both GSIs lag the base table until DynamoDB applies each write.

trade_offs.description: The expire-other-tokens update (query `36890455`) runs as a Query on TokensByUser followed by one UpdateItem per matching item; the scope condition (equal or NULL) and id inequality are filter expressions.
trade_offs.impact: A user has a handful of tokens, so the Query reads a few items and the updates are individual writes, not one set-based statement. The writes are not atomic as a group; a failed update is retried by the caller.

trade_offs.description: The retention delete (query `-805676`) is replaced by Time to Live on ttl_epoch, written only on items that are not confirmed and are expired, set to created_at plus 30 days and removed when a token is confirmed.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background within days of the expiry time and charges no write cost, so the scheduled DELETE and its Scan are gone. Expired items stay readable until deleted, which is harmless because the token lookup also checks confirmed and expired. The 30-day period is this design's value for the source's date parameter.

trade_offs.description: The token lookup by hash (query `54780307`) becomes a GetItem, with confirmed, expired, scope and created_at checked in the application.
trade_offs.impact: token_hash is unique, so the source's ORDER BY id LIMIT returns at most one row and the ordered scan disappears. The id generated by the source sequence stays as a plain attribute copied during migration; new ids are generated by the application.

trade_offs.description: The table has 97 rows and a design load of about 0.01 requests per second.
trade_offs.impact: Every table and index stays far below the per-partition limits of 3,000 read and 1,000 write units per second, so no sharding is needed. The row count is the collector's estimate.
